name: Bourbon
summary: A Capetian branch whose connection with the Albret family made the king of Navarre heir to the French crown.
origin: The Capetian House of Bourbon descended from Robert, Count of Clermont, a son of Louis IX, and his marriage to Beatrice, heiress of Bourbon. Their descendants took their name from her inheritance and established branches across France.
history: Their descendants divided into several branches. The Vendôme line produced Antoine of Bourbon, husband of Jeanne III of Navarre. Their son Henry inherited Navarre through his mother and attained the French crown in 1589 through his place in the Capetian succession.
legacy: The Bourbons maintained a presence in several European monarchies. The French branch gave rise to the reigning lines of Spain, Naples, Sicily and Parma, while Condé and Orléans retained their own estates and alliances.

name: Kotromanić
summary: The ruling house of the Bosnian banate and kingdom, connected with Serbia, Croatia and the Hungarian monarchy.
origin: Stephen I and Jelisava Nemanjić were the parents of Stephen II and Vladislav. Their descendants connected the Bosnian house with the Serbian monarchy and the Croatian nobility.
history: Elizabeth, daughter of Stephen II, married Louis I of Hungary. Tvrtko, son of Vladislav and Jelena Šubić, was crowned king in 1377. In later generations, the great Bosnian nobles intervened in the election and deposition of monarchs.
legacy: Stephen Tomašević married into the Branković family before ruling Bosnia. The Ottoman conquest of 1463 ended the monarchy, while members of its circle continued in exile.

name: Grand Comnene
summary: An imperial court on the Black Sea connected with Georgia and the Byzantine families.
origin: The Grand Komnenoi ruled Trebizond from 1204. Their imperial court was established on the southern coast of the Black Sea and developed close ties with Georgia and Byzantine aristocratic families.
history: Marriages with the Palaiologoi, Jakeli, Bagrationi and Kantakouzenoi extended across several generations. Trade with Genoa and Venice and relations with the powers of Anatolia shaped court politics.
legacy: The Ottoman conquest of 1461 ended the Empire of Trebizond. The marriages of its princesses had spread the ancestry of the Grand Komnenoi to Georgia, Constantinople and the courts of Anatolia.

name: Bogdana-Mușat
summary: Moldavian dynastic continuity encompassed rival branches, restorations and marriages with neighbouring courts.
origin: The Moldavian dynasty included several lines whose early origins and kinship remain debated. Stephen the Great and his son Petru Rareș occupied a central place in its alliances with neighbouring courts.
history: Petru married Elena Branković, linking the dynasty to the tradition of the Serbian despots. His daughter Chiajna, born of an earlier union, married Mircea Ciobanul of Wallachia. Ruxandra, Elena’s daughter, was consort of Alexandru Lăpușneanu and regent for Bogdan IV.
legacy: Petru’s two daughters connected different governments and demonstrate the importance of women in political continuity. Dynastic inheritance coexisted with the power of the boyars, intervention by neighbouring states and Ottoman overlordship.

name: Nemanjić
summary: The Nemanjić consolidated the Serbian kingdom and brought it to a brief imperial phase during the fourteenth century.
origin: Stefan Nemanja consolidated his authority in Raška during the second half of the twelfth century. His son Stefan received the royal crown in 1217. Another son, Sava, promoted the organisation of an autocephalous Serbian Church, recognised in 1219 and closely tied to the legitimacy of the house.
history: Successive brothers contested the throne and combined alliances with Byzantium, Hungary and Bulgaria. Dragutin retained northern domains after yielding the crown to Milutin. Dušan extended his power across Macedonia and other Byzantine regions and proclaimed himself emperor in 1346.
legacy: Dušan’s death in 1355 left Uroš V facing increasingly autonomous regional lords. His death in 1371 ended the Serbian imperial line. The foundations at Studenica, Žiča and Dečani preserved the dynasty’s memory through religious patronage, written culture and the formation of the medieval Serbian state.

name: Württemberg
summary: A comital house in Swabia transformed its scattered possessions into a duchy with Stuttgart as its political centre.
origin: The counts took their name from Württemberg Castle near Stuttgart. During the Late Middle Ages they acquired lordships and urban rights in Swabia. Eberhard IV’s marriage to Henriette of Montbéliard added an inheritance west of the Rhine.
history: The division of 1442 created the Stuttgart and Urach lines. Eberhard the Bearded reunited the territory through the Treaty of Münsingen in 1482. His marriage to Barbara Gonzaga connected his court with Mantua. Maximilian I elevated Württemberg to a duchy in 1495.
legacy: Ulrich temporarily lost power and recovered it in 1534 with Philip of Hesse’s help, afterwards introducing the Reformation. Later dukes governed alongside estates with significant fiscal powers. The family’s connections reached Russia through Sophie Dorothea, wife of the future Paul I, and other European courts.

name: Griffin
summary: The House of Griffin ruled Pomerania for centuries amid family partitions and pressure from its Baltic neighbours.
origin: The house took its name from the griffin on its arms. The first dukes consolidated their power in Pomerania during the twelfth century. Relations with Denmark, Brandenburg, Poland and the Empire shaped their autonomy and the division of the inheritance among branches.
history: The duchies of Szczecin, Wolgast and Słupsk underwent successive divisions and reunifications. Eric of Pomerania became king of the countries of the Kalmar Union. Bogislaw X reunited Pomerania in 1478 and strengthened administration, justice and coinage against urban and seigneurial powers.
legacy: The adoption of the Reformation transformed religious institutions and ducal property. The final branches reunited under Bogislaw XIV, whose childless death in 1637 ended the house’s rule. The Thirty Years’ War and subsequent settlements divided its lands between Sweden and Brandenburg.

name: Rákóczi
summary: Princes of Transylvania whose family alliances extended into Croatia and Hungary.
origin: George I and George II represent the house’s princely continuity in the seventeenth century. George II’s marriage to Sophia Báthory linked two families from the Transylvanian sphere.
history: Francis I was elected during his father’s rule but never assumed the principality. His marriage to Jelena Zrinski added Croatian ties. Francis II later led a war against the Habsburgs and received the Transylvanian title while control of the principality was disputed.
legacy: Francis II rejected the 1711 Treaty of Szatmár, which ended the war, and remained in exile. The loss of the principality shifted the family’s activity toward diplomacy and the search for support against the Habsburgs.

name: Přemyslid
summary: Bohemia’s first great ruling house transformed a principality into a kingdom that temporarily extended across Central Europe.
origin: The Přemyslids consolidated Prague’s power from the late ninth century. Some princes received personal royal titles. Ottokar I obtained a hereditary crown, confirmed by the Golden Bull of Sicily in 1212, and strengthened Bohemia’s position within the Empire.
history: Wenceslaus I and Ottokar II promoted towns, colonisation and mining. Ottokar II united Austria, Styria and other eastern territories before Rudolf of Habsburg defeated him in 1278. Wenceslaus II restored royal authority and also obtained the Polish crown.
legacy: Wenceslaus III had claims to Hungary and inherited Bohemia and Poland, but was murdered in 1306. The male royal line ended with him. His sister Elizabeth of Bohemia married John of Luxembourg and carried dynastic continuity to the new kings. A Přemyslid branch continued to rule in Opava.

name: Gedimide
summary: The dynasty of Gediminas expanded the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and founded lines that ruled several kingdoms of Central Europe.
origin: The family emerged among the Lithuanian rulers of the late thirteenth century. Gediminas, grand duke from 1316, expanded his lands and maintained diplomatic relations with cities, religious orders and other European powers. His correspondence connected Vilnius with these networks.
history: His sons Algirdas and Kęstutis shared the defence and expansion of the grand duchy. Their successors competed for power: Jogaila obtained the Polish crown through his marriage to Jadwiga, and Vytautas later consolidated his rule in Lithuania. Victory over the Teutonic Order in 1410 strengthened their position.
legacy: Jogaila’s branch gave its name to the Jagiellonians, kings of Poland and also of Bohemia and Hungary. Other descendants founded princely lines in Ruthenian and Russian lands. The marriages of Aldona to Casimir of Poland and Sophia to Vasily I of Moscow extended the house’s connections to its principal neighbours.

origin: Fulk V was Count of Anjou and father of Geoffrey, who married Empress Matilda. Geoffrey and Matilda were the parents of Henry II, establishing Plantagenet continuity in England.

legacy: Fulk V’s descendants spread across Anjou, England and Jerusalem. His son Geoffrey used arms bearing golden lions that became associated with the family’s memory.

summary: The Capetian House of Courtenay descended from Peter, son of Louis VI, and Elizabeth, heiress to the lordship of the first House of Courtenay.
origin: The marriage of Peter, son of Louis VI, to Elizabeth of Courtenay transmitted the name and lordship to a new Capetian line. Elizabeth belonged to the first House of Courtenay, which had established a branch in Edessa.
history: Peter II and his descendants attained the Latin Empire of Constantinople. The imperial title survived the loss of the city in 1261. Catherine of Courtenay transmitted it to her daughter Catherine of Valois, born of her marriage to Charles of Valois.
legacy: Catherine of Courtenay transmitted her imperial rights to the descendants of her marriage to Charles of Valois. The three roundels on the family arms preserved the memory of the Courtenay inheritance through its successive heiresses.

name: Toulouse
summary: The comital House of Toulouse built a major power in Occitania and established a branch in Tripoli. The Albigensian Crusade and the succession of 1271 transformed its lands.
origin: The Raimundine dynasty became established in Toulouse and Rouergue during the Middle Ages. Its estates grew through inheritance, alliances and seigneurial rights of various kinds.
history: Raymond VI and Raymond VII faced the Albigensian Crusade and intervention by the French monarchy. The peace of 1229 reduced the latter’s power and arranged the marriage of his daughter Joan to Alphonse of Poitiers, brother of Louis IX. In the eastern Mediterranean, Raymond III of Tripoli represents another path taken by the house.
legacy: Joan inherited Toulouse in 1249. Her death and that of Alphonse without issue in 1271 allowed the county to be incorporated into the French royal domain. The Occitan cross continued to identify Toulouse and Languedoc after the end of this comital line.
